transcript:
Header: 2026-12-27 10:00am PT | Duration: 1:02 | Recording: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Samira Nguyen (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (NovusAI CTO), Maya Lopez (NovusAI Lead ML Engineer), Jordan Kim (Head of AI), Priya Rao (Security), Ben (SRE)

Summary: Migration/demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together APIs to Redwood API, discussed differences in parameters, streaming, function-calling equivalents, embeddings, and enterprise requirements (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed next steps: send mapping doc, run benchmarks, schedule POC scoping.

[00:00] Alex Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving time before the holiday week, uh we'll keep it practical — quick agenda, parity mapping, console walkthrough, Optimize suggestions, and then bench next steps.
[00:18] Ravi Patel: Yeah thanks Alex, we've got a hard deadline end of Q1 to reduce cost and move off a multi-vendor setup, so looking for parity and minimal code churn.
[00:28] Alex Park: Totally. Samira, I'll hand it over to you for a quick mapping overview.
[00:33] Samira Nguyen: Cool thanks. So high level, NovusAI is calling OpenAI/Anthropic/Together now — we looked at their sample prompts — the main asks are text generation with streaming, structured tool calling, and embeddings. On Redwood side we map generation to /v1/generate, streaming is server-sent events, function/tool calling is supported via the structured output + annotations, embeddings are /v1/embeddings. We'll share a one-page parity table.
[00:58] Maya Lopez: When you say structured output, is that the same as Anthropic's system messages + JSON schema? We heavily rely on schema enforcement.
[01:06] Samira Nguyen: Yes the Redwood SDK and REST allow a schema param — we do best-effort validation and will optionally reject if output doesn't conform, similar to Anthropic:schema behavior, though internals differ. There's a small note about tokenization edge cases — we'll highlight those.
[01:27] Jordan Kim: How about function calling? We currently use OpenAI function-calling for tool routing, with name, args, and then we parse. Do you support automatic selection?
[01:36] Samira Nguyen: We support the same pattern — you declare tools in the request and the model returns either a direct answer or a tool call object. Redwood's console also has a live tool-execution trace in the routes view which helps debugging.
[01:50] Ben (SRE): We're concerned about latency tail and cold-starts — on OpenAI sometimes we see 300–500ms extra on cold starts. How does Redwood handle warm pools and KV cache?
[02:01] Alex Park: Good question. Redwood Dedicated has pre-warmed pools and continuous batching. Samira: the runtime keeps a persistent KV cache per session for long-context apps and there's configurable warm-up policies.
[02:13] Samira Nguyen: Right, and for cold-start mitigation we recommend pinning model instances for steady-state traffic or using a tiny reserved pool for burst traffic; we'll include recommended autoscale settings in the doc.
[02:26] Priya Rao: Security — we need assurance around encryption at rest, KMS, audit logs. Do you integrate with customer KMS/HSM?
[02:34] Alex Park: Yes, Private deployments support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; Dedicated can integrate with customer KMS in many setups. We'll share SOC2 and KMS integration guides.
[02:45] Priya Rao: Also need network controls — VPC peering or private endpoint?
[02:48] Samira Nguyen: Private supports VPC peering and on-prem installs if needed. Dedicated offers private endpoints inside your cloud VPC.
[02:58] Ravi Patel: Ok good. On the parity front, we want to minimize code changes. For example, OpenAI parameters like temperature, top_p, stop sequences — how direct is the mapping?
[03:09] Samira Nguyen: Very direct. Temperature, top_p map 1:1. stop sequences work similarly. The only gotcha is that our tokenizer counts slightly differently for some special tokens, so prompt-length heuristics might need minor tweaks. We'll flag tokenization differences in the spreadsheet.
[03:26] Maya Lopez: For embeddings we currently send 512-d floats — is the embedding dimension the same? We use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small.
[03:35] Samira Nguyen: Redwood offers multiple open-model embeddings; we can match dimensionality in most cases or recommend equivalently performing models. We'll include benchmarked cosine similarity vs your current embeddings.
[03:48] Jordan Kim: About cost — what levers do we have? Quantization? batching?
[03:52] Alex Park: Redwood Optimize gives suggestions — quantization profiles per model, intelligent batching and caching. For embeddings you can enable partial caching and reuse for recent user queries. Pricing will have per-token and per-embedding rates; we'll send an estimate for your traffic.
[04:08] Maya Lopez: Demo time — can we see the API call shape and SDK example?
[04:12] Samira Nguyen: Yep. I'll share my screen. (screen share) On the left is a sample REST call: POST /v1/generate with body: model, input, temperature, max_tokens, stream true. Response streaming comes as SSE events with data: {"type":"delta","content":"..."}. For function calls you add tools: [{name:"lookup", schema:{...}}].
[04:40] [04:40] Samira Nguyen (cont): Notice headers: Authorization: Bearer <key>, X-Redwood-Account. SDKs are available in Python/Node/Go.
[04:50] Maya Lopez: Our current handlers assume OpenAI-style response objects with choices[0].message.content. Will adapting to Redwood be a large diff?
[04:57] Samira Nguyen: Minimal — SDKs emulate the familiar shapes; we also provide middleware to translate OpenAI shapes to Redwood shapes for a transitional period. We'll include a code snippet that returns OpenAI-compatible payloads.
[05:12] Ben (SRE): What about tooling for model rollouts — can we canary new model versions?
[05:17] Alex Park: Yes, rollouts and routing policy is in the Console — you can set traffic splits, canaries, automatic fallback to lower-latency variants.
[05:26] Jordan Kim: For internal evals we run automated regression tests on outputs. Does Redwood support eval hooks or prompt-based monitors?
[05:34] Samira Nguyen: Redwood Optimize has a quality monitoring pipeline — you can attach prompt sets, store baseline outputs, and trigger regression alerts. It ties to your routes so you can see which model or rollout caused the regression.
[05:48] Maya Lopez: About latency benchmarks: can we run a side-by-side with our current Tailor profile? We have a batch of 2000 prompts with mixed lengths.
[05:56] Samira Nguyen: Absolutely. For the POC we'll spin up a Dedicated test pool with similar GPUs and run synthetic and real request replay. We'll provide CSV outputs with P50/P90/P99 latencies and token cost.
[06:08] Alex Park: Next I'll show the Console briefly — routes, tracing, and cost breakdown.
[06:13] Samira Nguyen: (screen) Here's the routes page; each route shows token usage, cost per token, and a breakdown by model variant. The trace view shows request timeline: client recv, batching wait, kernel exec, post-process.
[06:28] Maya Lopez: Can we get token-level breakdown per user? We need per-tenant billing.
[06:33] Samira Nguyen: Yes, you can tag tokens at route level and get token-level, user-level breakdown; we also support token quotas per API key and per-route limits.
[06:43] Priya Rao: Auditing — does the console store raw prompts by default? We need options to redact or not persist inputs.
[06:50] Alex Park: You control retention and redaction policies. Private deployments can be configured to never persist raw prompts. Dedicated can have configurable retention windows and automatic redaction.
[06:59] Ravi Patel: Ok good. Are there migration libraries or scripts? We have a custom wrapper that normalizes across models — would be nice to have helpers.
[07:08] Samira Nguyen: We have an OpenAI compatibility layer: a small middleware that maps OpenAI request/response to Redwood; it covers streaming, function calls, and embeddings. We'll include the repo link in follow-up.
[07:20] Jordan Kim: Licensing and SLA — for Dedicated what uptime SLA do you offer?
[07:25] Alex Park: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs in enterprise agreements; exact numbers depend on contract tier — we'll provide the SLA doc.
[07:34] Ben (SRE): Any niceties around k8s or infra? We want to keep observability in our existing stack.
[07:40] Samira Nguyen: Redwood exposes tracing hooks and logs to external systems — you can forward traces to Datadog/Tempo and logs to your S3 or Splunk.
[07:49] Maya Lopez: Regarding Together models, some of our prompts call the Together-chat model which has slightly different system message handling. Any pitfalls?
[07:58] Samira Nguyen: Together's system-role vs user-role conventions differ; we'll include mapping examples. The main conversion is preserving the intent of system messages and converting chat history arrays to Redwood's context param.
[08:10] Alex Park: Quick callout on token accounting: when you migrate, expect a 1–3% delta in token counts due to tokenizer implementational differences, especially with non-ascii and prompt templates.
[08:21] Ravi Patel: Fine, as long as it's predictable.
[08:24] Maya Lopez: Can we see a live demo of streaming and a function call?
[08:28] Samira Nguyen: Yep — I'll run a quick streaming generation with a tool call to our sample "kb_lookup".
[08:33] [08:33] Samira Nguyen (typing) POST /v1/generate { model: "rwd-3b", input: "Summarize user doc and call kb_lookup if needed", tools:[{name:"kb_lookup", schema:{query:string}}], stream:true }
[08:49] [08:49] SSE events start: data:{"type":{"delta":true},"content":"Sure — here's a short summary..."}
[09:05] [09:05] SSE event: data:{"type":"tool_call","tool":"kb_lookup","args":{"query":"user doc 123"}}
[09:12] Samira Nguyen: Then the tool is executed and the model receives the tool result and continues. After tool execution the final event has type:"final" with structured output.
[09:22] Maya Lopez: That flow looks compatible.
[09:25] Priya Rao: One more security nit: can we disable tool execution in production and force manual approval?
[09:31] Samira Nguyen: Yes, there's a per-route policy to block automatic tool execution and surface tool calls for manual review.
[09:39] Alex Park: Ok we're at about 35 minutes — want to recap and assign owners.
[09:45] Ravi Patel: Recap: parity mapping, benchmarks, security pack, POC scoping. Timeline: aim to start benchmarks in the first week of Jan and POC through January.
[09:56] Samira Nguyen: I'll follow up with the parity spreadsheet and middleware repo. Alex will send the pricing estimate and proposed Dedicated test pool plan.
[10:04] Alex Park: Great. Any final Qs?
[10:07] Jordan Kim: Just one — do you support model quantization options for 4-bit at inference?
[10:12] Samira Nguyen: Yes, we have quantization profiles and Redwood Optimize recommends them when quality impact is acceptable. We'll include quantization tradeoff notes for your models.
[10:20] Maya Lopez: Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[10:22] Alex Park: Thanks all. We'll send the mapping doc today and the benchmarks invite — talking offline about exact GPU shapes. Happy holidays.
[10:30] (call ends)
